reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Chorea gravidarum is a descriptive term for any chorea arising during pregnancy, not a single disease entity; it reflects an underlying predisposition unmasked by the hormonal state.
Historically most cases followed prior Sydenham chorea or rheumatic fever, but with declining rheumatic disease, antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus are now leading causes.
Onset is typically in the first half of pregnancy and often remits spontaneously after delivery or termination.
A comparable oestrogen-related mechanism produces chorea with combined oral contraceptive use, supporting a hormonal trigger.
Chorea may be unilateral or generalised and can be severe enough to interfere with feeding, sleep and safety.
A prior episode strongly predicts recurrence in subsequent pregnancies or with oestrogen exposure.
Thorough evaluation for an underlying secondary cause is mandatory, as management and prognosis depend on the aetiology rather than the pregnancy itself.
Treatment is reserved for disabling symptoms, favouring the lowest effective dose of agents with the most reassuring gestational safety profile after specialist counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: Chorea gravidarum arises when the physiological rise in oestrogen and progesterone during pregnancy sensitises or unmasks striatal dopaminergic pathways in a predisposed individual. Oestrogens are thought to modulate dopamine receptor sensitivity within the basal ganglia, and in those with prior basal ganglia injury (notably previous Sydenham chorea) or circulating antibodies (antiphospholipid or anti-basal ganglia antibodies in lupus), this heightened dopaminergic responsiveness precipitates dysfunction of the striatal indirect pathway. The resultant reduction in inhibitory output produces disinhibited involuntary movements. The frequent postpartum remission mirrors the fall in sex hormone levels, and the same mechanism explains contraceptive-induced chorea.
additionalInvestigations: Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I)
Antinuclear and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies for lupus
Anti-streptolysin O / anti-DNase B titres and echocardiography if rheumatic history
Serum caeruloplasmin, copper and slit-lamp examination for Wilson disease
MRI brain (used selectively, with appropriate gestational precautions)
redFlags: Features of antiphospholipid syndrome such as thrombosis or recurrent pregnancy loss requiring anticoagulation assessment
Systemic features of active lupus (rash, arthritis, nephritis, cytopenias)
Severe chorea threatening maternal exhaustion, rhabdomyolysis or fetal wellbeing
New neurological or cardiac signs suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Hyperthyroid crisis features accompanying the chorea
reference.prognosis: Chorea gravidarum usually remits after delivery or termination and carries a good prognosis when no serious underlying disorder is present, although it commonly recurs in later pregnancies or with oestrogen exposure. Overall outlook is determined by the underlying cause, particularly antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus.
pitfalls: Regarding chorea gravidarum as a benign self-contained diagnosis and failing to investigate for antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus.
Overlooking a missed antiphospholipid syndrome that also endangers the pregnancy through thrombosis.
Prescribing dopamine-blocking drugs without specialist counselling on gestational safety.
Missing thyrotoxicosis or Wilson disease as reversible contributors.
Not advising on recurrence risk with future pregnancies and oestrogen-containing contraception.
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Movement Disorders in pregnancy - standard neurology reference reviews
management: Treat the unmasked underlying disorder — anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy with rheumatology input for antiphospholipid syndrome, immunosuppression for lupus, and antistreptococcal and rheumatic follow-up where prior Sydenham chorea is implicated
Withdraw oestrogen exposure by stopping combined oral contraceptives and counselling against oestrogen-containing preparations, as this often abolishes the chorea

Reserve symptomatic dopamine-blocking or dopamine-depleting agents such as a typical neuroleptic or a benzodiazepine for chorea severe enough to threaten feeding, sleep or safety, choosing agents with the most favourable pregnancy-safety profile
Provide supportive care with a safe environment to prevent injury and attention to nutrition, hydration and rest during the hyperkinetic phase
Monitor for spontaneous remission after delivery or termination and for rheumatic carditis with echocardiography when a rheumatic aetiology is suspected
Coordinate joint obstetric, neurology and rheumatology care with a maternal-foetal medicine plan for delivery
Counsel about the high likelihood of recurrence in future pregnancies or with later oestrogen exposure
